name: 2 Maccabees
sourceNote: Translated fresh from the Greek text of 2 Maccabees in H. B. Swete's edition of the Septuagint (Cambridge, 1909; public domain), with Brenton's public-domain English version consulted as a check. The book was composed in Greek; after two prefaced letters to the Jews of Egypt (1:1–2:18), it presents itself as an abridgment of a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene. Dates are given by the Seleucid era; each is converted in the text to its year BC, with the modern month span for any named month, and the original reckoning is in a footnote. Converted years may be off by one, since the era was reckoned from autumn 312 BC in some sources and from spring 311 BC in others. Weights and sums of money are given in approximate modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes; ancient standards varied. Greek kyrios is translated "Lord" and theos "God." Verse numbers follow the standard English versification. This is a draft awaiting scholarly review.

verses.text: To their kindred, the Jews throughout Egypt, greetings from their kindred, the Jews in Jerusalem and in the land of Judea: true peace.
May God do you good, and may he remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants.
May he give all of you a heart to worship him and to carry out his will with a great heart and a willing spirit.
May he open your hearts to his law and commandments, and may he give you peace.
May he listen to your prayers and be reconciled with you, and never abandon you in a time of trouble.
Here and now we are praying for you.

In the reign of Demetrius, in the year 143 BC,{a} we Jews wrote to you: “During the suffering and crisis that fell on us in those years, after Jason and his supporters betrayed the holy land and the kingdom,{b}
they set fire to the gateway and shed innocent blood. Then we pleaded with the Lord and were heard; we offered sacrifice and fine flour, we lit the lamps, and we set out the loaves."
And now see that you keep the days of Booths in the month of Chislev (in November–December).{c}

Written in the year 124 BC.{d} From those in Jerusalem and Judea, the senate, and Judas, to Aristobulus, who is of the stock of the anointed priests and tutor to King Ptolemy, and to the Jews of Egypt: greeting, and health.{e}
Having been rescued by God from grave dangers, we give him great thanks, as men who stood in battle array against a king.
For it was he who hurled out those who drew up for battle against the holy city.
When the leader reached Persia with an army that seemed irresistible, they were cut to pieces in the temple of Nanea through a trick employed by Nanea's priests.{f}
On the pretext of marrying the goddess, Antiochus came to the place with his Friends, meaning to take its great riches as a dowry.
The priests of Nanea had laid out the treasures, and Antiochus went inside the walls of the sacred area with a small escort; as soon as he was in, they locked the temple.
Opening a secret door in the paneled ceiling, they hurled stones and struck down the leader as if with thunderbolts; then they cut the bodies in pieces and threw the heads to those outside.
Our God be praised in all things, he who gave up the impious to judgment!

We are about to keep the cleansing of the sanctuary on the twenty-fifth of Chislev (in November–December), and so we judged it needful to make this known to you, that you also may observe a feast of Booths and of the fire which appeared when Nehemiah, the builder of the sanctuary and altar, brought up sacrifices.{g}

For when our ancestors were being led away to Persia, devout priests of that time secretly took some of the fire from the altar and hid it in the hollow of a dry cistern, where they made it secure, so that the place was unknown to anyone.
After many years had passed, when it pleased God, Nehemiah, sent by the king of Persia, dispatched the descendants of the priests who had hidden the fire to recover it.

They told us they had found no fire, only a thick liquid. He ordered them to scoop some up and bring it. After the materials for the sacrifices had been laid on the altar, Nehemiah commanded the priests to splash the liquid over the wood and everything on it.
When this was done and some time had passed, and the sun, which had been behind clouds, shone out, a great blaze flared up, so that everyone marveled.
And as the offering burned, the priests made prayer, both priests and all the rest, Jonathan beginning and the others answering, as Nehemiah did.
The prayer went like this: "O Lord, Lord God, Creator of all things, awe-inspiring and strong, just and merciful, you alone are King and kind,
you alone are bountiful, you alone are just, almighty, and eternal. You rescue Israel from every evil; you made our ancestors your chosen ones and consecrated them.
Receive the offering for the whole of Israel your people; keep safe your inheritance and sanctify it.
Bring our dispersion together again; free those in bondage among the Gentiles; regard the scorned and abhorred; and so let the Gentiles learn that you are our God.
Punish those who oppress us and insolently abuse us in their arrogance.
Plant your people in your holy place, as Moses said."
Then the priests sang the hymns.
Once the sacrifice was burned up, Nehemiah gave orders to pour what remained of the liquid upon some large stones.
When this was done, a flame blazed up, but it was consumed by the light that shone back from the altar.{h}

Once the affair came to light, the Persian king was told that where the priests carried into exile had concealed the fire, liquid had been found, and that Nehemiah's company had used it to purify the offerings.
The king fenced off the place and made it sacred, after investigating the matter.
And to those on whom the king bestowed favor, he gave a share of the many gifts he received.{i}
Nehemiah's company gave this the name nephthar, interpreted as "cleansing"; but among most it goes by the name naphtha.{j}

notes.text: Greek: in the 169th year (Seleucid era). The Seleucid era is the reckoning used in the books of Maccabees, counted from the founding of the Seleucid kingdom in autumn 312 BC or spring 311 BC; converted years may be off by one. Demetrius is Demetrius II.
Jason the high priest; see 4:7–26 and 5:5–10.

Literally "the days of Booths of the month of Chislev," that is, the festival of the temple's rededication (Hanukkah), kept for eight days in the manner of Booths; see 10:6. Chislev is the ninth month, November–December.
Greek: in the 188th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:7). Many interpreters attach this date to the first letter; others take it as the opening of the second letter.
Aristobulus was a Jewish philosopher of Alexandria; the king is probably Ptolemy VI Philometor. The second letter (1:10–2:18) claims to come from Judas Maccabeus and so would date from about 164 BC.

Nanea (Nanaia) was a goddess worshiped in Persia and Mesopotamia. This account of the death of Antiochus differs from 1 Macc 6:1–16 and 2 Macc 9; it may reflect the death of Antiochus III in 187 BC, who died plundering a temple in Elymais.
Chislev is the ninth month, November–December. The traditional reconstruction of the temple was by Zerubbabel and Joshua (Ezra 3–6); this tradition credits Nehemiah.
The sense of this verse is uncertain.
Or "the king took many gifts and gave a share to them"; the Greek is obscure.
Nephthar is of uncertain origin and meaning; the explanation "purification" is the author's. Naphtha is a flammable petroleum liquid.

verses.text: The records show that the prophet Jeremiah instructed those being taken into exile to take some of the fire with them, as already described,

and that the prophet, having handed them the law, charged the deportees not to forget the Lord's ordinances, nor to be led astray in their thoughts on seeing images of gold and silver and their finery.
With other such words he exhorted them never to let the law depart from their hearts.
The writing also told how the prophet, warned by an oracle, ordered the tent and the ark to go along with him, and how he went out to the mountain that Moses had climbed to view God's inheritance.{a}
Arriving there, Jeremiah found a cave-like dwelling, and into it he carried the tent, the ark, and the altar of incense; then he blocked up the entrance.
Some of his companions came up afterward meaning to mark the way, but they could not find it.
When Jeremiah learned of this, he rebuked them: "Unknown that place will be, until God brings his people together in one assembly and mercy comes.

Then the Lord will reveal where they are, and the Lord’s glory and the cloud will appear, just as they were displayed in the days of Moses, and when Solomon prayed that the place would be wonderfully consecrated.”
It was also made clear how Solomon, being endowed with wisdom, offered a sacrifice for the dedication and completion of the sanctuary.
Just as Moses prayed to the Lord and fire came down from heaven and devoured the sacrifices, so too Solomon prayed, and the fire descended and consumed the whole burnt offerings.
And Moses said, "Because the sin offering had not been eaten, it was consumed."{b}
Likewise Solomon too kept the eight days.{c}

The same things are also recorded in the archives and in Nehemiah’s memoirs, which add that he founded a library and gathered the books about the kings and the prophets, the writings of David, and the kings’ letters about gifts dedicated to God.{d}
In the same way Judas also gathered up all the books that had been scattered because of the war that befell us, and we have them in our possession.
So if you need any of them, send people to fetch them for you.
Since, then, we are about to celebrate the purification, we write to you. You will do well, therefore, to keep these days.
It is God who has saved all his people and has given back to all the inheritance, the kingship, the priesthood, and the consecration,

as he pledged in the law. Our hope rests on God, that he will be quick to pity us and to gather us from everywhere under heaven into the holy place; for out of great evils he delivered us, and he cleansed the place.
The story of Judas Maccabeus and his brothers,{e} the purification of the great temple, and the dedication of the altar,
and further the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator,{f}

and the manifestations from heaven granted to those who strove valiantly, with honor, on behalf of Judaism,{g} so that, few as they were, they overran the whole land and chased off the barbarian multitudes,

and won back the temple renowned throughout the inhabited world, and set the city free, and reestablished the laws then on the verge of being overthrown, the Lord in all his gentleness being merciful toward them,
all this, made known by Jason the Cyrenian in five books, we will try to shorten into one composition.
For we saw the flood of figures, and the difficulty that the sheer mass of material poses for anyone wishing to plunge into the narratives of the history,
and we have aimed to bring delight to those who wish to read, ease to those inclined to commit things to memory, and benefit to all who come upon the work.
For us who have taken on the toil of abridging, the task is no easy one; it is a matter of sweat and sleepless nights,
just as it is no light thing for one preparing a banquet who seeks the enjoyment of others. Even so, for the sake of the gratitude of many, we shall gladly endure the toil,
leaving to the original author the precise treatment of every detail, while we exert ourselves to follow the outlines of an abridgment.

For as the master builder of a new house must concern himself with the entire structure, while the one who undertakes to paint and decorate it must look into what is suitable for adornment, so I judge it to be in our case.
To enter into the subject, to range over it in discussion, and to busy oneself with particulars is the task of the first compiler of the history;
but the one who recasts it must be allowed to aim at brevity of expression and to forgo exhaustive treatment.
So at this point let us begin the narrative, adding only this much to what has been said; it would be foolish to go on at length in the preface and then shorten the history itself.

notes.text: Mount Nebo; see Deut 32:49; 34:1–4.
See Lev 10:16–20.
"Votive offerings": gifts dedicated to the temple.
Maccabeus, the surname of Judas, perhaps means "hammer" (Aramaic maqqaba), but the meaning is uncertain.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes ("God manifest") and his son Antiochus V Eupator ("of a noble father").
This is the earliest known use of the Greek word "Judaism," the name for the Jewish way of life; compare 8:1; 14:38.

verses.text: The holy city lived in complete peace and the laws were observed with great faithfulness, thanks to the devotion of Onias the high priest and his loathing of evil,{a}
and so the kings themselves honored the place and enhanced the temple with magnificent gifts,
so that even Seleucus, king of Asia, met from his own revenues all the costs connected with the service of the sacrifices.{b}
But a certain Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin,{c} who had been appointed captain of the temple, fell into a dispute with the high priest about the regulation of the city market.
Unable to prevail over Onias, he went to Apollonius son of Thraseas, who at that time was governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia,{d}

and informed him that the treasury in Jerusalem was overflowing with immense amounts of money, too much to count, and that it had nothing to do with the sacrificial accounts but could come under the king’s control.
When Apollonius met the king, he told him of the money that had been disclosed to him. The king chose Heliodorus, his chief minister, and sent him with orders to carry off the reported wealth.{e}
Heliodorus at once took the road, in appearance to visit the towns of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, but in reality to accomplish what the king intended.

On arriving at Jerusalem and being kindly welcomed by the high priest of the city, he laid before him the information that had been given and made plain why he had come, and he asked whether these things were really so.
The high priest explained that there were deposits belonging to widows and orphans,

and that some belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man holding a very eminent place. So far was it from what Simon, that ungodly man, alleged. The whole came to fifteen tons of silver and seven and a half tons of gold.{f}
It was completely unthinkable to wrong people who had trusted in the holiness of the place and in the sacredness and inviolability of a temple honored all over the world.
But Heliodorus insisted, because of the king’s orders, that the money had to be seized for the royal treasury in any case.
Fixing a day, he went in to manage the examination of these funds, and anguish of no small degree gripped the entire city.

The priests flung themselves down before the altar in their priestly robes and cried out to Heaven, to the one who had laid down the law concerning deposits, asking him to preserve these intact for those who had placed them there.
Whoever looked on the high priest's countenance was pierced in mind, for his appearance and his altered complexion revealed the agony within his soul.
Fear and a shuddering of the body had spread over him, and by these the grief settled in his heart was made evident to the onlookers.
Crowds of people also ran out of their houses to join in a public plea, because the holy place was about to be disgraced.

The women, with sackcloth bound beneath their breasts, filled the roadways in great numbers; and of the virgins kept in seclusion, some ran to the gateways, some to the walls, and some leaned out to look through the windows.
And all of them, stretching out their hands toward heaven, made their entreaty.
It was pitiable to see the multitude prostrate in a mixed throng, and the anxious expectation of the high priest in his great anguish.
While they were calling upon the almighty Lord to keep the things entrusted safe and secure for those who had entrusted them,
Heliodorus went on with what had been decided.

But when he was already present at the treasury with his guards, the Ruler over spirits and every power made a great appearing, so that all who had dared to come along were struck with dismay at God's might and gave way to weakness and fear.

For a horse appeared to them, carrying a terrifying rider and decked with the most beautiful harness; charging violently, it lashed at Heliodorus with its forefeet, and the one mounted on it seemed to wear a full suit of golden armor.
Two other young men also appeared to him, remarkably strong, splendid in beauty, and gorgeously dressed; they stood on either side of him and flogged him without pause, inflicting many blows on him.
When he had suddenly fallen to the ground and was enveloped in deep darkness, they picked him up, put him on a stretcher,
and carried away the man who had just entered that treasury with a great retinue and all his bodyguard, now helpless; and they plainly recognized the sovereign power of God.
So he, by God's working, lay cast down, voiceless and bereft of every hope of rescue,

while they blessed the Lord who had wondrously glorified his own place; and the sanctuary, so lately brimming with dread and confusion, was now full of joy and rejoicing, since the almighty Lord had shown himself.
Soon certain of Heliodorus's intimates asked Onias to call on the Most High and grant life to the man who lay at his very last gasp.
The high priest, fearing that the king might suspect that some foul play had been done to Heliodorus by the Jews, offered a sacrifice for the man's recovery.

As the high priest was offering the sacrifice of atonement, those same youths, clad in the same garments, once more appeared to Heliodorus. Standing there, they said, "Owe Onias the high priest much thanks; on his account the Lord has granted you life.
As for you, scourged from heaven, proclaim to everyone God's mighty strength." When they had said this, they were seen no more.
Heliodorus then offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made extravagant vows to the one who had spared his life; he said goodbye to Onias and marched his troops back to the king.
He bore testimony to everyone of the deeds of the supreme God that he had seen with his own eyes.
The king asked Heliodorus who might be a fit man to dispatch once again to Jerusalem, and he answered:

"Should you have some foe or someone scheming against the state, dispatch him there, and you will receive him back well scourged, if indeed he comes through alive; for truly a power of God surrounds that place.
The one whose abode is in heaven is himself its overseer and helper, and those who arrive there to do it harm he smites and destroys."
This was the outcome of the affair of Heliodorus and the protection of the treasury.

notes.text: Onias III, high priest about 196–175 BC.
Seleucus IV Philopator, king 187–175 BC.
Some ancient witnesses read "of Bilgah," a priestly family (Neh 12:5, 18).
Coelesyria ("Hollow Syria") was the region between the Lebanon ranges, extending in official usage to Palestine.
Literally "the one in charge of affairs."
Greek: four hundred talents of silver and two hundred talents of gold. A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg).

verses.text: But the aforesaid Simon, who had turned informer against the funds and against his own homeland, went about slandering Onias, as if it were Onias who had stirred Heliodorus up and had been the author of these evils.
He dared to call the city's benefactor, the protector of his fellow countrymen and zealous upholder of the laws, a conspirator against the state.
When the enmity advanced so far that even murders were carried out by one of Simon's trusted agents,
Onias saw how dangerous the rivalry was, and that Apollonius son of Menestheus, governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, was fanning Simon's malice.{a}
So he betook himself to the king, not as an accuser of his fellow citizens but with an eye to the welfare, both public and private, of all the people.
For he saw that without the king's attention it was impossible for public affairs to find peace, and that Simon would not cease from his folly.
When Seleucus died and Antiochus, known as Epiphanes, took the throne, Jason, the brother of Onias, got the high priesthood through bribery,{b}
promising the king in a petition about thirteen and a half tons of silver, and from some other revenue about three tons more.{c}

Besides this he engaged to pay in writing about five and a half tons further, if leave were given him by the king's authority to found a gymnasium and a training corps of youths, and to register the people of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch.{d}
The king agreed; and as soon as Jason held the office, he immediately moved his countrymen over to the Greek way of life.

He set aside the royal privileges granted to the Jews, obtained through John the father of Eupolemus, who had gone on the embassy to the Romans for friendship and alliance;{e} and abolishing the lawful ways of life, he brought in new customs contrary to the law.
With relish he founded a gymnasium right below the citadel, and he made the noblest of the young men submit to wearing the broad-brimmed hat.{f}
Thus Hellenism reached its height and the adoption of alien customs advanced, through the boundless profanity of Jason, an impious man and in no way a high priest,

that the priests were no longer eager for the services of the altar. Despising the sanctuary and neglecting the sacrifices, they hastened, once the gong summoned for the discus, to take part in the unlawful exercises provided in the wrestling school.{g}
Counting their ancestral honors as nothing, they prized Greek distinctions above all.
For this reason a grievous calamity overtook them, and the very people whose ways they envied and wished to resemble in every respect became their enemies and punishers.
For to act impiously against the divine laws is no light matter, as the period that follows will show.
When the games held every fifth year were being celebrated at Tyre, and the king was present,{h}

the polluted Jason sent official delegates, purporting to be Antiochenes from Jerusalem, conveying nearly three pounds of silver for the sacrifice to Heracles.{i} But the bearers themselves thought it unfitting to spend it on a sacrifice,
and so, on account of those bringing it, it went to the construction of warships.{j}

Apollonius son of Menestheus was dispatched to Egypt for the enthronement of King Philometor,{k} and Antiochus, discovering that Philometor had turned unfriendly toward his interests, looked to his own safety. So he went to Joppa and from there came down to Jerusalem.
He was received in grand style by Jason and the city and was ushered in with torchlight and shouting. After that he marched his army into Phoenicia.
After three years, Jason sent Menelaus, brother of the Simon mentioned above, to deliver the money to the king and to finish the records on urgent business.{l}
But Menelaus, once presented to the king, flattered him with the bearing of a man of power and so drew the high priesthood to himself, outbidding Jason by about eleven tons of silver.{m}
After receiving the king's commission he returned, bringing nothing worthy of the high priesthood but having the passions of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast.
So Jason, who had undermined his own brother, was undermined in turn by another and was driven as a fugitive into the land of Ammon.
Menelaus kept firm hold of the office, but of the money promised to the king he paid nothing in due order.
Sostratus, the citadel's commandant, pressed for payment, for the collecting of the dues belonged to him; and on this account both men were called before the king.
Menelaus left his own brother Lysimachus as his deputy in the high priesthood, and Sostratus left Crates, the commander of the Cypriots, in his place.{n}
Matters standing thus, the citizens of Tarsus and Mallus rose in revolt, since their towns had been handed over as a gift to Antiochis, a concubine of the king.
So the king went off in haste to settle matters, leaving as his deputy Andronicus, a man of high rank.

Menelaus, supposing a favorable moment had come, purloined certain golden vessels belonging to the sanctuary and made a present of them to Andronicus; others he had already sold off in Tyre and the neighboring towns.
When Onias had clear knowledge of this, he exposed him publicly, having withdrawn to a place of sanctuary at Daphne near Antioch.{o}

Therefore Menelaus, taking Andronicus aside, urged him to kill Onias. Andronicus went to Onias, and resorting to treachery, gave him his right hand with oaths. Though still suspected, he persuaded Onias to come out from the sanctuary, and at once he shut him away and killed him, with no regard for justice.{p}
For this reason not only Jews but many people of other nations too were indignant and displeased at the unjust murder of the man.
On the king's return from the districts of Cilicia, the city's Jews appealed to him, joined by Greeks who shared their loathing of wrongdoing, concerning the senseless slaying of Onias.
Antiochus was grieved at heart and moved to pity, and he wept because of the moderation and great good conduct of the deceased.

Blazing with anger, he immediately took off Andronicus’s purple robe and ripped his clothes off, then led him through the whole city to the very spot where he had committed the crime against Onias; there he killed the murderer, as the Lord paid him back with the punishment he deserved.

When many sacrileges had been committed in the city by Lysimachus with the connivance of Menelaus, and the report had spread abroad, the populace gathered against Lysimachus, for many of the gold vessels had already been carried off.

As the crowds were rising and becoming filled with rage, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and began unjust violence, with a certain Auranus leading, a man advanced in years and no less in folly.

When the people saw the attack of Lysimachus, some seized stones, some thick pieces of wood, and others grabbed handfuls of the ashes lying near, and they hurled them in wild confusion at Lysimachus and his men.
As a result they wounded many of them, struck down some, and put all of them to flight; and the temple robber himself they killed beside the treasury.
A charge was brought against Menelaus over these matters.
When the king came to Tyre, the three men sent by the council of elders presented the case before him.
But Menelaus, already losing, offered Ptolemy son of Dorymenes a substantial sum if he would bring the king round.
So Ptolemy, taking the king aside into a colonnade as if for fresh air, induced him to change his mind.
Menelaus, the cause of all the evil, he acquitted of the charges, while the unfortunate men, who would have been freed as innocent even if they had pleaded before Scythians, he sentenced to death.{q}
So those who had pleaded on behalf of the city, the country districts, and the sacred vessels swiftly underwent that undeserved punishment.
For this cause Tyrians too, out of abhorrence of the wickedness, bore the cost of their funeral with great generosity.
Yet Menelaus kept his office through the covetousness of the powerful, ever thriving in wickedness, set up as the great traitor to his fellow citizens.
